en: 8. Section on the Causes and Conditions for Receiving Precepts (Part 1 of 3). Section Eight: The Causes and Conditions for Receiving Precepts; Appendix: The Method of the Six Mindfulnesses for Renouncing Precepts.
Now, one who receives the precepts transcends the defiled stream of the vulgar and base, entering the precious rank of the noble assembly.
Since one's aspiration grows ever more expansive, the objects of focus likewise become more numerous; because the objects of focus are so many, the practice of the Dharma becomes difficult;
and because it is difficult to comprehend, the principle requires careful and detailed examination.
Yet worldly sentiments and defilements constantly obscure the teachings;
to serve as a teacher or a master is both easy and difficult.
This is simply because people follow established customs as if they were natural, failing to reflect upon what should be maintained or reformed.
Indulging in such ignorance, they disrupt the true teachings.
Some merely cling to the literal text and recite it with diligence, yet remain ignorant of its underlying characteristics;
others have been hindered by prior obstacles and are thus incapable of fulfilling the duties of the Saṃgha.
In some cases, the boundaries of the *sīmā* are loosely defined, resulting in a lack of clear demarcation;
in others, the number and quality of the monks are insufficient, making it impossible to inspire faith;
and in yet others, robes and alms bowls are borrowed, which is inherently contrary to the Dharma.
Such a master is difficult to serve with sincerity;
to receive instruction in vain and waste one's efforts is to labor in vain for a lifetime.
If later generations act likewise, there will be no end to their time of bondage.
Therefore, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states:
"After my parinirvāṇa, there will be no one who fulfills the precepts.
These words must certainly be true; they require profound and careful deliberation.
Once received, it is difficult to reverse; thus, it is not appropriate to receive it again.
Therefore, I shall provide a detailed exposition so that practitioners may rely upon it according to their capacities.
First, I clarify the fulfillment of conditions for receiving the precepts; subsequently, I add the instructional teachings.
Regarding the five conditions for the beginning and middle [stages]: first, there are five types of those capable of receiving [the precepts].
The first is the human realm.
Because it is received among human beings, and it is difficult for it to be accomplished in other realms.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If one is less than seventy years of age and unable to perform the necessary tasks, one may not receive [the precepts]."
If one has exceeded seventy years of age, the time for leaving the household life has passed; it is entirely unsuitable.
This is explained in detail in the "Dharmas of the Śrāmaṇera.
Second, the faculties must be complete.

This refers to the body being possessed of various evils, such as illnesses, deafness, blindness, and the hundred and odd types of impediments extensively listed in the Vinaya; none of these are in accordance with the Dharma.
Applying this standard to seek [the truth], it is certain that those who are deaf, mute, or insane will not receive the precepts.
As for others, there is a general confusion regarding whether they obtain them or not, as explained in the *Yichao*.
Third, the purity of the vessel of the three bodies (*trikāya*).
This means that from the time one is an ordinary person until just before receiving ordination, one is free from the thirteen impediments (*antarāyika-dharma*) and other such faults.
Fourth, the possession of the characteristics of renunciation.
The Vinaya states:
"One should shave the head and don the kashāya; one is equal to those who have left the household life.
This is the fifth of the dharmas for obtaining a small portion [of merit].
This refers to having previously received the ten precepts.
The Vinaya states:

"If one does not confer the śrāmaṇera precepts upon a person but confers full ordination (upasampadā) instead, that person obtains the precepts [of ordination], while the officiant incurs an offense."
The second category of objects of engagement consists of six types.
First is the accomplishment of boundary-delineation (*sīmā-bandha*),
which, as it relies upon ritual action (*karmavācanā*), must necessarily conform to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
If the rite is not properly performed, the subsequent dharma will not be established.

Therefore, one must clearly understand the characteristics of the boundaries (*sīmā*), skillfully discern right from wrong, and investigate who originally established them; only when one has ascertained that there is no confusion may one rely upon them as a standard.
Otherwise, one must relinquish what was previously established and re-establish them anew.

In recent times, people have frequently failed to follow established procedures, instead arbitrarily establishing small boundaries outside the monastery to receive ordination; this is contrary to the Dharma, as has already been clarified above.
If there is indeed such a necessity, it is not erroneous to establish a large boundary.
According to the *Vinayamātṛkā*, if one merely establishes a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) without encircling it with a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), the precepts cannot be received.
Among the masters of the Central Kingdom, there is great respect for the practice of conferring the precepts through ritual action.
Therefore, in the biographies, whenever there was a recipient [of the precepts], they mostly performed the ritual by boat upon the river.
When people asked the reason for this, they replied:
"Those who establish the boundary (*sīmā*) according to the Dharma are few; I fear that if the assembly is incomplete or the rite is improper, the reception of the precepts will not be accomplished."
Other matters may be rectified later, and their failure to be accomplished does not entail many faults;
however, for one who wishes to perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas and serve as a field of merit for the world by receiving the full precepts, it is improper to be negligent or reckless.
Therefore, when one stays in a quiet place, the task will certainly be accomplished.
Second, there must be a Sangha capable of upholding the Dharma;
for the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is not something that can be performed by an individual alone.
The threefold recitation must be completed according to the Dharma;
if even one person is missing, it is contrary to the Dharma and the Vinaya.
What is meant here by "fewer" does not refer to the number of heads being incomplete.
This refers to those who perform the ritual at the improper time, or when the assembly is incomplete or the procedure is contrary to the Dharma, as clarified in the *Pārivāsika-vastu*.
The text states:
"From this day forward, ten monks shall confer full ordination (*upasampadā*)."
This is based on the regulations for China.
In frontier regions where there are no monks, it is provisionally permitted for five people who uphold the Vinaya to confer ordination;

however, if monks are later present, one must follow the original rules for conferring the precepts. Those who receive the precepts [under the former rule] or incur offenses [for failing to do so] are as set forth in this *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
All within the four boundaries gather together in harmony.
As the text says:
"There is no other means by which one may obtain a separate assembly."

Fifth, there is the teaching of the formal motion with four announcements (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), which eliminates inversions, omissions, transpositions, unclear explanations, and so forth. Sixth,
the requisite conditions are fully provided.
In the text, it is stated that if one lacks the robe and bowl, or borrows them, it does not constitute the formal reception of full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Thirdly, regarding the formal request for ordination upon generating the resolve:
the text says:
Because that which does not beg and that which lacks intention are not established [as such].
The fourth is the correspondence between mind and object.
As the text says:
In cases such as those who are asleep, intoxicated, insane, or unconscious, the mind does not engage with the object.
Furthermore, the text states:

"If the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* is performed incorrectly according to the rules for a motion (*jñapti*), or incorrectly according to the rules for a formal act (*karman*), and if the preceding assembly acts contrary to the Dharma, it does not cause the recipient to give rise to [the necessary] mental state; this is precisely what is meant by the object not corresponding to the mind."
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha* states:
"If one receives [the precepts] with a sincere and reverent mind, there is non-informative action (*avijñapti*);
if one receives them with a casual mind, there is only the informative action (*vijñapti*), but no non-informative action."
The fifth matter is brought to completion.

Beginning from the invitation of the preceptor and ending with the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations), throughout these nine stages of interaction, there is not the slightest discrepancy.

The boundary is not one where the assembly is divided, the Sangha is not deficient in number, and the *karman* is without fault. When the recipient’s mind is fully resolved, the ordination is accomplished.
That which contradicts the above constitutes what is not the Dharma (*adharma*).
Now, I shall cite scriptural evidence.
The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states:
Five conditions must be fulfilled for its accomplishment:

first, the preceptor (upādhyāya) must be in accordance with the Dharma; second, the two ācāryas must be in accordance with the Dharma; third, the seven bhikṣus must be pure; fourth, the *karmavācanā* must be successfully performed; and fifth, the Saṃgha must be in harmony and grant their consent (*chanda*).
The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Regarding those who receive [precepts]: if one is a layperson, one receives the five precepts or the eight precepts; if one has left the household life, one receives the ten precepts.

If one violates even one of the grave offenses among the five precepts, one cannot receive the eight precepts, nor can one receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), nor act as a preceptor (*upādhyāya*)."
This is subsumed under the first of the thirteen difficult points (*trayodaśa-dūṣaṇa*).
Since there must be one who receives [the ordination], and based on the preceding conditions, such a person would certainly be incapable; thus, it is not permitted by the holy teaching.
Second, regarding the addition of the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*), this is divided into two parts:
First is the expedient means of the causal origination; second is the clarification of essence and function.
As for the methods of the *saṃgha-karman* (formal assembly), they are as set forth in the preceding section; however, because the matter is of great importance, they are explained here once again.
Regarding the conditions for this, there are ten.
First, does the recipient obtain the Dharma?
As clarified in the Fourfold Vinaya, one must first possess the ten precepts before being permitted to receive full ordination.
In the text, it is stated that if one does not confer the ten precepts, the assembly of monks incurs an offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says:
"The reason the ten precepts are established is for the purpose of habituating oneself to the Buddha-dharma; they are not to be received all at once, as is the practice of non-Buddhists."
The Buddha-dharma is not like this; it is like the great ocean, becoming progressively deeper as one enters it.
Second, the method for requesting a teacher.
First, the request for the *upādhyāya*.

By this means, one obtains the root of the precepts; if such a person were absent, there would be no way to receive and practice them. Lacking guidance, they could not grow together; therefore, it is essential to invite them.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
Because they do not request [instruction], they frequently commit unrighteous acts; when various masters reprimand them, they respond in turn, "Who requested the Venerable One to be my preceptor?"
The Buddha therefore established this rule:
if one has not been invited, one must not accept;
to receive [an offering] under such circumstances constitutes an offense.
In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, regarding the request for the Dharma, it does not state that the Sangha must be in a secluded place.
Judging by reason, if one requests in advance while in a separate location, what harm is done to the great principle?
As for those currently within the assembly, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:

Have the person receiving the precepts first enter the Saṃgha; instruct them to prostrate themselves, head to the ground, and pay obeisance to each member of the Saṃgha one by one, and only then request [the preceptor].
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"Now, from the Honored One, I seek the Upādhyāya, etc."
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"When requesting a preceptor (*upādhyāya*), one should cup his feet with both hands.
One should perform the preparatory rites as described above and, having approached the preceptor, a bystander shall instruct him, saying:"
"The reason I request you, Preceptor, is that this is the very root of receiving the precepts and the place to which one turns for refuge.
Having thus responded according to the disciple's capacity, [the Master said]: "Based on what you yourself have stated, you do not understand; therefore, I shall instruct you!"
The text says: "Venerable One, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!

I, [Name], now request the Venerable One to be my preceptor (*upādhyāya*). May the Venerable One act as my preceptor; by relying upon the Venerable One, I shall receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*)."
"Out of compassion!
[Recite this] three times. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"After the assembly has made the request three times, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) should speak to inspire joy in that person."
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: He replied, “So be it!”
"I instruct you: be pure and do not be negligent!
The disciple replied: "I shall receive and uphold this upon my head!"
In the following text, there are ten further methods of answering.
Question:
Since the request has already been made during the time of the śrāmaṇera precepts, why is it requested again now?
Answer: Because there is a change in status, one does not rely on the original teacher;

furthermore, when he was a śrāmaṇera, he requested ordination and was initially received for the ten precepts, whereas now that he is a śrāmaṇera, he is being received for full ordination (*upasampadā*), and thus the methods of reception differ.
It may be that the Upādhyāya lacks the requisite virtue and is thus unfit to provide formal sponsorship;
therefore, two pairs are requested.
Next, the two masters are requested.
There is no explicit textual authority in the Vinaya.
According to the *Buddha-abhidharma*, there is also a ritual for requesting [the precepts], but as its phrasing is neither elegant nor superior, it has not been excerpted here.
One should therefore follow the precedent of the Preceptor and request them collectively.
One should approach the preceptor with full decorum, while an attendant instructs them, saying:
"The Karmavācanā Preceptor Ācārya is the primary condition for receiving the precepts;
if this person did not uphold the noble Dharma, there would be no way for the wholesome dharmas of the Dharmadhātu to arise."
"Therefore, one must cultivate a mind of supreme reverence before the preceptor of the precepts in order to give rise to the non-informative [action].
Having spoken thus in various ways, he instructs:
"Venerable One, attend to me with a single mind!"

I, [Name], now request the Venerable One to serve as my *karmācārya*. May the Venerable One act as my *karmācārya*; through reliance upon the Venerable One, I shall receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
"Out of compassion!
[Recite this] three times. Next, request the instructor (*ācārya*).
Having likewise performed the preparatory practices as before, an attendant instructs, saying:
"It was because of this person that you were instructed, guided, and enlightened;
it was through him that you were led to the Saṃgha to receive full ordination;
the skillful means of the causal origination all depend upon this teacher."
"Only when the request for the essential points has been made shall the precepts be conferred.
The text is the same as the ritual of the *karmavācanā* master, with the sole difference being that the *śikṣamāṇācārya* acts as the instructor.
Next, the seven witnessing masters are requested.
The principle must be based on formal request (*yācanā*).
Since the *karmavācanā* rite is not to be performed alone, one must necessarily select this person to serve as a witness to ensure there is no error or deviation.
According to the correct standard of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is logical and consistent to request [the witness] in this manner.
Thus, when the recipient generates wholesome states, the former teacher’s mind is honored;
since both parties are in harmony, how could this not be the same Dharma?
Yet in the world, many do not practice this, but instead cause the Dharma to perish.
If one discusses the merit of generating the precepts, it is equal to that of the three masters; why then not request them?
One may follow the precedent of the three masters and request them before the great assembly; as for the number of monks, there is likely no fixed limit.
To further clarify the characteristics of whether the ten preceptors have fulfilled their requirements, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:

"If a disciple knows that the upādhyāya has violated the precepts, knows that one should not receive [ordination] from such a person, and also knows that even if one were to receive it, the precepts would not be obtained; [yet he still ordains him, he commits an offense]."
If one possesses such knowledge, then the formal reception [of the precepts] is not accomplished;
conversely, it is accomplished by the opposite.
Regarding the remaining nine masters, there are no explicit texts in the Vinaya, but they may be understood by analogy.
If the preceptor commits a grave offense and the *karmavācanā* master knows of it, the ordination is likewise not accomplished;
this is because it is recognized that the person being nominated is unfit to be a bhikṣu.
If any among the ten masters mutually know that a grave offense has been committed, the rite is also not accomplished.
Furthermore, one must understand that if a transgressor is known to have committed an offense, they may not dwell together;

yet it is not known what specifically constitutes such an exclusion. According to the Vinaya texts, if a disciple knows that their preceptor has broken the precepts, the gravity of the offense remains unclarified.
To explain this in detail according to its meaning: even one who has committed a *duṣkṛta* offense does not successfully receive the precepts.
Because such a person has violated the rules of decorum (*airyāpathika*), they do not possess the virtue required of a teacher;
knowing that the precepts cannot be obtained, yet receiving them by force, they are not successful because they lack the requisite intention.
Since one must ensure that both seeing and hearing are pure, one must select [the preceptor] in advance; as the text says:
"one should cause him to be selected.
Regarding the virtues of a *upādhyāya*, they vary and differ; those enumerated in the Vinaya number more than one hundred and thirty kinds.
The single category of "ten summers" must necessarily be strictly defined;
other virtuous characteristics are as described in the "Dharma of Teacher and Disciple.
Therefore, a preceptor with only nine summers incurs an offense when conferring ordination.
Regarding the two types of ācāryas, those with five or more summer retreats (varṣa) are mentioned in the Vinaya as being "generally more than five years" [of seniority].
For other teachers, it depends on the number of their summer retreats.
To clarify the significance of the teacher: if there are venerable elders of great virtue, then goodness will arise in future generations.
The *Five Hundred Questions* states:
If a bhikṣu who has not yet completed five years of ordination ordains a disciple, and he does so knowing it is improper, he commits a *pāyattika* offense;
however, if the disciple is unaware of whether it is right or wrong, they still receive the precepts.
If one knows [this], one does not obtain the precepts.
The *Vyākhyāyukti-ṭīkā* states:

"If one has already completed five years of summer retreat (*varṣa*), one may serve as a witness (*sākṣin*) and as a teacher of deportment (*airyāpathika-ācārya*) for the conferral of the full ordination (*upasampadā*)."
Once seven years of summer retreat have passed, one may serve as a *karmācārya*.
Since this is a position of teacherhood, one must not sit on the same bed with another.
These are the three conditions for the arising of the precepts through instruction.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:

"In the ritual for receiving the precepts, one first expounds the Dharma to guide and enlighten the recipient, causing them to give rise to a mind of compassion toward all objects; thus, they attain the higher training in ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*)."
The text is thus; yet, seeking the meaning through its substance, it first clarifies the objects of conditions and subsequently clarifies the measure of the mind.
Regarding the former, the characteristics of the precepts that are generated are indeed immeasurable.
Because prior to receiving the precepts, evil pervaded the entire Dharma-realm;
now, desiring to advance and receive them, one overturns those former evil objects and gives rise to wholesome thoughts.
Therefore, the cause from which the precepts arise likewise pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
If one were to discuss this according to its various objects, a separate commentary would require more than thirty sheets of paper;

yet, to summarize it, it does not exceed the categories of sentient and non-sentient beings, the two truths of emptiness and existence, the principle of cessation and nirvana, the holy teachings spoken by the Buddha, written texts and scrolls, images, stupas, and temples, and the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness.
Taking the entire dharma-realm as its measure, all of these constitute the substance of the precepts.
Therefore, the *Śāṅghabhadra-śāstra* states:
"Because sentient beings are infinite, the precepts are also infinite.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā* states:
It is not merely regarding sentient beings that one obtains immeasurable [retribution];
it is also so for the vast earth of the ten directions, extending downward to the realm of space.
If one harms even as much as a speck of dust within it, one incurs the corresponding guilt.
Now, translated as "precept-virtue" (jie-shan), it therefore extends across the land.
Thus, the *Śāṅghabhadra* (*Shansheng*) says:
"The great earth is boundless, and the precepts are likewise boundless."
Grasses and trees are immeasurable, the waters of the ocean are boundless, and space is limitless; the precepts are likewise equal to these.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
"A person who has newly received the precepts is equal in virtue to the Buddha’s precepts."
Inferring from this, the monastics and nuns who have left the household life are truly a gathering of merit and wholesome dharmas;
that their status is honored above both humans and devas is precisely due to this.
Whether they have received the precepts or maintain them fully, their merit is difficult to enumerate.
Even if one violates them, the benefit remains boundless.
Thus, the *Daśacakra-sūtra* states:
"A bhikṣu who has broken the precepts, though he be a dead man;"
The residual power of this precept is still able to demonstrate the path of human and celestial realms, just as in the analogies of ox-gallstone, musk, and incense.
The Buddha therefore spoke these verses:
"Though the *campaka* flower has withered, it surpasses all other flowers;"
"Even bhikṣus who have broken the precepts are superior to the various non-Buddhists.
Therefore, for a practitioner, one who has broken the precepts possesses immeasurable merit and has a distant prospect of liberation;
whereas one who does not receive the precepts follows the current into the sea of suffering, never attaining release.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"It is better to receive the precepts and then break them— entering hell first and attaining liberation later—
than for one who has not received the precepts to continue wandering through the three realms."
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also states:

"Even though one may attain the body of a Brahmā deity, or even reach the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception, at the end of one's life, one will still fall back into the three evil realms."
This is precisely because of a lack of precepts that one undergoes such cycles of coming and going.
Thus, according to the capacities of individuals, the teachings are presented in either extensive or abbreviated forms to bring about awakening and understanding;
if one does not understand this, the mind will be restless and obscured, the precepts will not be received, and one will merely cause suffering for oneself and others in vain.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śīla-sūtra* states:
"If the mind is sincere and profound, then non-informative action (*avijñapti*) arises;
if it is light, it does not arise."
How could one allow for such empty excess? In principle, one must be profoundly earnest.
Next, have them generate the precepts.
One should say: "You should generate the superior grade of mind, so as to obtain the superior grade of precepts."
If one possesses an inferior grade of mind, even up to the level of an Arhat, their precepts are of an inferior grade.
The *Vibhaṅga-vinaya* states:
"I now resolve my mind to seek the Way and shall teach all sentient beings; yet all sentient beings cherish their own lives."
Receiving [the precepts] by means of this matter involves a mind of inferior and weak capacity; although one may obtain the Buddha's precepts, they are still not superior.
To clarify the remaining two grades according to their meaning:
what is the middle grade?

If one says, "I now direct my mind toward the Path with sincerity to resolve the doubts of sentient beings; I act as a bridge and ferry for all, being able to benefit myself and others alike, and I uphold the true precepts."
What is the superior grade?

It is when one says: "I now resolve to arouse the mind and receive the precepts in order to fulfill the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*), to enter the three gates of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*), and to rightly seek the fruit of *nirvāṇa*;
furthermore, by means of this Dharma, I shall guide sentient beings to reach *nirvāṇa* and cause the Dharma to abide for a long time."
Even such an aspiration is still a mistaken conception;
how much more so for one who does not aspire at all, who certainly lacks any sense of reverence or esteem.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
Ordinary beings, when first beginning their study, speak from within a mind of delusion;
those who have attained the fruit of *anāgāmin* speak from within a mind of conceit;
and those who have attained the fruit of *arhat* speak only by way of names and designations.
Thus, by knowing for oneself the limits of the mind, one also attains the limits of the Buddha’s pure precepts.
Therefore, the text says:
"The sons of the Buddha are likewise; they diligently seek the root of the Brahma-precepts," and so forth.
Question:
To which vehicle does this teaching belong,
such that one develops the aspiration for the Mahāyāna?
Answer: This four-part school (Caturvarga-nikāya) is, in its meaning, equivalent to the Mahāyāna.
As the text of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states:

If there are those who, for their own sake, desire to seek the Buddha-way, they should respect the true precepts and dedicate them to all sentient beings so that together they may achieve the Buddha-way.
There are many such authentic examples within the Vinaya.
Master Guang also judged this to fall within the scope of the Mahāyāna Vinaya.
Thus, regarding the object of the precept-generating conditions and the mind possessing supremacy—
these two paths must necessarily be received at the prior time through the instruction of a wise teacher.
One must cause the mind to flow in continuous succession so that the perception of objects is clear and pure;
one should not wait until the last moment to speak of generating the resolve.

If the instruction from the teacher is given only at the last moment, even the characteristics of the dharma will be hollow and superficial; how then could it enable the recipient to attain the superior grade?
Or if none at all arise, would this not be a grave matter?
Fourth, the Vinaya states:
"When establishing a person to receive the precepts, place them in a location where they are within sight but beyond earshot."
If the person receiving the precepts is out of earshot or sight, or if they are outside the boundary (*sīmā*) and so forth, it does not constitute the conferral of full ordination (*upasampadā*).
One stands out of earshot for fear that they might hear the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual proclamation);
yet, fearing this might still be contrary to the Dharma, one remains within the sight of the Saṃgha.

In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, because it addresses the arising of faults, it permits the establishment of the boundary (sīmā) outside the ordination platform (*śīla-maṇḍala*) within sight, and so forth.
The text of the *Caturvargika-vinaya* states: "Outside the boundary, one asks about the obstacles and impediments (*antarāyika-dharma*)," and so on.
At present, those who receive [the instruction] mostly remain within the boundary (sīmā); this is logically unobjectionable and accords with the superior scriptural texts.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"The instructor should [position himself] at a place that is neither too near nor too far," and so forth.
If many people receive [the precepts] together, they should be stationed in two places:
first, where many people walk and stand so that they may see the Sangha and give rise to a sense of reverence;
second, where those who are to be questioned are placed, apart from the Sangha and apart from the walking area of the śrāmaṇeras, to inquire into the circumstances there.

It is also permissible for them to be in the same location; however, fearing that they might later ask questions as before without due respect, one should have each person put on their seven-strip robe (saptaka) and other garments with the seams facing outward, and have them stand there.
Regarding the appointment of a Master of Decorum (*airyapatha*) by means of a single formal motion (*jñapti-karman*):
